title: The systems approach
log: 2026-10-27T01:00:11Z write: the API refused it in the chapter request, so it is written on its own next

match.reason: No existing point teaches the systems approach of inputs, transformation and outputs adapting to the environment; the closest points cover what a business is or its environments, which are related but different ideas.

draft.title: The systems approach
card: The systems approach sees a business as a system: a set of connected parts that work together. A change in one part can affect the others.
A system takes in inputs, such as labour, materials and money. It transforms them through its processes and produces outputs, such as goods and services.
A business is also an open system. It takes in resources from its environment and sends outputs back to it, so it must keep adapting as that environment changes.
A manager using this approach looks at how the parts fit together, such as production, marketing and finance, rather than treating each one alone.
draft.remember: A business is a set of connected parts that turns inputs into outputs and keeps adapting.

a.q: Which example is the transformation step in a bakery run as a system?
opts: Staff turn flour and eggs into loaves of bread
The owner buys flour and eggs from a supplier
Customers buy the loaves from the shop counter
A new café opens next door and takes some customers
a.why: Transformation is the process that turns inputs into outputs, and baking does that. Buying flour is an input, which is tempting because it is part of the production chain but it is not the step that changes the inputs.
a.clue: Look for the step that changes inputs into something new.

b.q: A furniture maker in Orange buys cheaper timber to cut costs. Quality drops, customers return items, and the service team is swamped. Which idea of the systems approach does this best show?
opts: A change in one part can affect other parts
Workers should be paid only for their output
Each department should act on its own
Groups inside the business compete for power
b.why: The change in buying affected quality and then customer service, so the parts are connected. Acting on its own is tempting but is the opposite: the example shows that a department's choices spill into other parts.
b.clue: Follow the effect of the purchasing choice through the business.

a.best: Staff turn flour and eggs into loaves of bread

b.best: A change in one part can affect other parts

check.summary: No problems found. The card matches the systems approach as the syllabus describes it, and both questions each have one clearly correct answer.
